comments.author: jrflo
comments.text: This trend is pretty shocking to me. I assumed that we had moved beyond cross-entropy loss being important with the increasing use of RL, it's wild that the trend is so clear. Really nice to have such a simple benchmark instead of the increasingly convoluted ones that are getting spun up every day. Also, I wonder what happened with GPT 4.5? I think o1 was the start of true reasoning models, right? I was using Claude at the time so I can't remember.

comments.author: ACCount39
comments.text: Interesting that GPT-4.5 is the only discontinuity on the graph. The oversized monster LLM has performed worse than CoT-trained o1 and o3 on the benchmarks, so CoT + RL clearly provided better "real world performance" improvements - let alone "price/performance." But if pre-training perplexity on held-out data really does measure something like "base model IQ" or "base model g factor", then it does support the hypothesis that 4.5 still had more "intellectual potential" than the o-series. So, if you were wondering why do AI companies train 10T+ monsters now, and are taking aim at 100T too? It's because scale works.

comments.author: tensor
comments.text: I'm a bit skeptical about the claim that particular abilities "emerge" at given perplexities. For instance, there are smaller models that are specifically trained on math, and I imagine those models have much higher general perplexity on other tasks. On the other hand, assuming you have appropriate training data for a task , then yes obviously perplexity is going to measure performance on that task. Being able to predict the next task token is obviously going to be a near perfect correlation with accuracy on the task.

comments.author: x313
comments.text: I thought perplexity on simple text data has been saturated for a while (as in perplexity is uncorrelated to task success - ex. https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23771v2 ). I suspect what's happening is their test dataset is actually just something really hard, like math papers or something. In that case perplexity would just be a direct measure of math knowledge, which means this blog would just be saying that better math knowledge predicts better math skills.

comments.author: rcr-anti
comments.text: That GPT 4.5 result indicates to me that such a number does not, in fact, give a useful, portable benchmark for capability. If we stopped at pretraining, yeah. But we don't, that was the big thing about GPT 4.5, aka Orion, originally meant to be GPT 5. It might have been a better compressor/predictor, but that didn't make it useful. The cynical part of me wonders what OpenAI suspects or knows the equivalent figures for the other closed labs.

comments.author: Avamander
comments.text: For the price and complexity of building a good Linux-based time server I'd heavily recommend looking at FPGA-based solutions instead. x86 platforms also have PCIe PTM and TGPIO options available[0], which are tad better than the common ARM equivalents and GPIO interrupts. In general Pi-s are relatively bad for timekeeping. Not just the NIC (which can be replaced by hats with their own), there are also oscillator replacement mods[2] to work around this to some extent. Though all this still leaves many other sources of timekeeping error. So if the goal is low-cost precise timekeeping, one can assemble something FPGA-based[2] for quite a bit less money, that can reach very low noise figures. You can spend the remaining money on the GNSS antenna and receiver instead. I'm also sure a FPGA-based approach could be taken even further with some external timekeeping chips available and the FPGA could just do the NTP/PTP protocol stuff. [0]: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxK0_j2Ah2I [1]: https://raspberrypi.stackexchange.com/questions/74482/switch... [2]: https://fy.chalmers.se/~f96hajo/fakernet/board_Arty_A7-35-GP...

comments.author: imoverclocked
comments.text: I think digital social networks should be somewhat disparate. IRL social networks are already self-islanding by their nature of formation via shared interest. Cross-pollination happens when individuals are part of multiple networks. Let’s take two different social networks today: Strava and Threads. They serve wildly different purposes and have no need to talk with each other. By virtue of hyperlinks, one can enable cross-posting between networks if that is somehow desirable. The only way a shared protocol makes sense is if the purpose of the network is either very general (looking at you, e-mail) or the semantics involved are very homogeneous. This proposal wants federation but also doesn’t say how existing federation technologies fail much less how their own will work. E-mail will be hard to unseat and social networks are still a dime a dozen with wildly different expectations for messages passed between them.

comments.author: jph
comments.text: There's low-hanging fruit IMHO by testing using semantic naming vocabulary with semantic error vocabulary. Example macro: assert_approx_eq_with_relative_error!(a, b, err). It's a semantic name that explains more about what it does, and the macro also provides a test failure message that guides the developer, or an AI, toward fixes and documentation. I wrote the Rust crate Assertables to help with this. See https://crates.io/crates/assertables . What I learned is writing semantic testing can help many more kinds of higher-value testing. As a specific example described by the article, I use enumeration testing for proving the UK National Health Service Number validator in Rust is accurate i.e. the test literally checks every number, then I can write tests such as assert_valid_nhs_number("111 111 1111").

comments.author: rkagerer
comments.text: Way too much caution in this thread. I've done all kinds of programming including embedded and full stack (from before the latter was even a colloquialized term). I absolutely love the degree of control you can get at the microcontroller level. One of my proudest projects had IRQ handlers written in assembly where I counted instruction cycles in order to guarantee worst-case latencies and well-defined impact to realtime activities in the main loop. There were also some lower-priority tasks going on that were cooperatively multitasked. Some time later I wrote a JavaScript library that mimicked some of those cooperative multitasking concepts to queue background image downloads and other generic "ITasks" in a manner that maximally utilized available connections (which were extremely limited by servers back then) and allowed on-the-fly reordering. The frontend used it to always ensure whatever image the user was most interested in (i.e. tiny previews, and large version of the result presently hovered over or that we anticipate will be hovered next) came up as close to instantaneous as we could get, and the rest of the large images lazy-loaded in an intelligent order. The result was an experience that felt so much faster than how most other websites operated back then (and ironically even now as bloat has really slowed a lot of sites down), and users loved it. So the concepts you learn at one end of the spectrum can definitely benefit you at the other. I have much less fun now that so much of the web has moved to React and other cookie cutter frameworks where the level of control comes at a higher cost (in terms of learning curve, understanding all the layers of abstraction, and space for developer creativity). In other words, just get in there and start playing with a personal project or two, and trust your instincts and all the experience that honed them!

comments.author: ferguess_k
comments.text: I'd say just do it. You have been in the industry for 15+ years and you surely know how to network/do interviews. I feel that you are just hesitating or wait for some confirmations. I wrote similar posts so that's my guess, but please criticize me if I'm wrong. My point is, whoever has actually done the transition, their experience may not really help you a lot. They might have a cousin who actually refers them to the company; They might have worked 10 years of embedded projects as a hobby; They might be lucky because 5 years ago there were a huge opening somewhere. I heard of a metaphor about elevators -- Several people ride an elevator to floor 100, and a reporter asked them how they get there -- one of them said he did 1,000 push-ups, another said he read 2 books, and a third said he bumped his head against the elevator's walls. Those experience might be very well relevant, or not. But above all, copying others' experience, in THIS market, probably doesn't work. Now that you are 6 years senior than me regarding SWE experience, I think you already know what to do -- just do it.

comments.author: tptacek
comments.text: I started my career in C/C++ and have done a fair amount of embedded work. In terms of actually doing stuff, there has never in the history of the world been a better time to do low-level and embedded systems work. The right advice here: find a project, scrounge the parts, and have an agent do basic bring-up work for you. If your last serious C work was 15 years ago, I think you'll be astonished how quickly you can progress to the "rewarding" part of any project. If your question is instead how you make a career transition to embedded/firmware work, that's much trickier. The obvious concern is AI's impact on the job market, but I'm chiming in to observe that this isn't the biggest problem with a web->embedded transition. Good jobs doing embedded stuff, at least for people who don't already have a pedigree doing that work, has for as long as I can remember been a bottleneck for people wanting to do this stuff. There's simply a lot more high-level work to be done than low-level work. I can see bright spots potentially ahead; I'm not a big Jevon's Paradox person but one kind of clearly Jevon-y area is hardware, because we've zorched one of the biggest impediments to getting new projects off the ground. But it hasn't happened yet, and might not.

comments.author: nik_s
comments.text: I think the layman's perception of the increase in survival (~13 months versus ~6 months) will make this look underwhelming. Nevertheless, it's important to remember that the incentives for clinical trials is to only include very late-stage patients who have exhausted all other options (faster trials, smaller sample sizes, surrogate endpoints, a shot at accelerated approval, ...). The fact that a treatment shows promise for these patients that are often in very poor health and considered "hopeless" by today's medicine is exceedingly rare, and the signal from this trial is indeed strong. The (somewhat reasonable) hope is that patients 1. with earlier forms of pancreatic cancer (non-metastatic) 2. that can undergo surgery 3. together with a (neo)adjuvant treatment with these kras inhibitors, will end up having a much lower recurrence rate and a chance for a long, healthy life. I think this is genuinely good news worth celebrating!

comments.author: mft_
comments.text: For once, this isn’t hyperbole. Metastatic pancreatic cancer hasn’t had a meaningful new treatment in literally decades - it’s been brutal chemotherapy or slightly less brutal chemotherapy. The new generation of KRAS inhibitors, of which daraxonrasib is just the first to make it to approval, is genuinely a practice-changing breakthrough. It won’t cure people with metastatic disease, but it will help a lot live better lives for longer.

comments.author: responder41
comments.text: RAS is a (class of) proteins in the membrane of your cells that are important in telling cells when it is time to grow. These proteins cycle between an "active" state that stimulates growth and an "inactive" state that doesn't. An extremely common genetic mutation that happens as a person develops cancer causes some of these cells to start making RAS proteins that do not correctly switch back to the "inactive" state. The cells with these mutations then grow and divide very rapidly and can become a tumor. Daraxonrasib works by binding the active state RAS proteins and preventing them from signalling and triggering growth. This can help prevent the tumors from growing further and potentially even shrink them as they are attacked by the immune system or other medication. (I'm not an expert, just a fan of knowing how things work, anyone can correct me if they know better)

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text: If you're new to quantized models: Don't get too excited about claims of fitting large models into tiny RAM footprints from random GitHub repos. There is always a tradeoff, and it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbers and even single benchmark scores. Just because you can get something to run on a device doesn't mean it's going to be useful. The headline claim of this repo (12X better) doesn't even apply to Inkling-2-Mini This repo's README is a mess of different histories as the author bounces from one popular model to the next. It refers to vague things like "the 1.2GB file" that probably made sense in an early vibecoding pass, but are now lost after the repo has been pushed around to different popular models. The truth is that random GitHub repos with messy READMEs almost never hold a real secret that the mainstream quantizations have missed. I would recommend sticking to mainstream quantizations like the official GGML release, Unsloth's quants, or the more well known community quantizers like bartowski or AesSedai. They typically follow an optimized size-quality tradeoff so you can find the one that fits your needs. When you see a repo like this where everything is so obviously vibecoded that the README is a rambling mix of projects and claims, you should probably go looking for a more authoritative source. The local LLM communities get spammed with 10 of these types of projects per day but I have yet to see a real breakthrough come from any of the vibecoded ones. The real work is coming from people who study this and have compute to test at scale or work on implementing advanced techniques which require inference engine support, like trellis quants.

comments.author: ptx
comments.text: The LLM-generated writing is incredibly tedious to read, but I like the idea of pre-loading the application and then forking the workers (kind of like Android's Zygote), while, as the LLM puts it, "Muru also takes care to freeze the garbage collector's view of the preloaded objects before forking", or, as it's more concisely put in the code, "gc.freeze()". A variation on that theme that I would like to try is forking a worker per user (or per session), which would be sandboxed (e.g. with Capsicum in FreeBSD) and only have access to that user's credentials. A separate process would route requests to these per-user workers and provide them with the appropriate credentials. This could then be combined with PostgreSQL's row-level security, with each user having their own user in PostgreSQL, and the per-user worker only having access to that particular user's database credentials. I feel like this should significantly limit the consequences of both SQL injection vulnerabilities and RCE vulnerabilities. It wouldn't solve stored XSS, I suppose, but I believe that is handled by using a template language for HTML (one that encodes parameters automatically on output). It also probably wouldn't scale to a planet-scale mass-market web application, but there are lots of apps that don't need that kind of scale but do need to be secure. Maybe this sort of thing has already been done and written about (by humans)?

stories.title_en: Notes on the discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
stories.title_ja: Notes on the discrete Fourier transform (DFT)

comments.author: perlgeek
comments.text: DFT works great if you have a single with equal spacing in the time domain (e.g. you have a microphone, and you measure the signal every 1/20k s or so). If that's not the case, rather than interpolating into a time grid, it's often better to use a generalization of the DFT called the "Lomb-Scargle Periodogram". For example if you have a periodic process like measuring the distance between two planets, but you only get measurements at random timestamps, that's the way to go. See for example https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/timeseries/lombscargle.ht...

comments.author: abnry
comments.text: There are four Fourier Transforms: 1. The (traditional) Fourier Transform for real-domain functions. 2. The Discrete Time Fourier Transform (DTFT) for integer-domain function. 3. The Continuous Time Fourier Transform (CTFT) for unit circle-domain (or periodic) functions, also known as Fourier Series decomposition. 4. The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for finite integer domain functions. You might say there are only three of these transforms because 2 and 3 are essentially, but not quite, inverses of each other. But really there is only one Fourier transform. In a few senses actually. There's character theory which unites them all based on the (topology and group structure of the) function domain. So reals, integers, unit circle, and finite integers are the function example domains. But another way they are all united is with distributions and dirac delta functions. The dirac comb is very important for understanding it. Any time you have a discrete series, represent it as dirac impulses and apply the normal Fourier Transform (operating on distributions) maps it to the other transforms. You can represent the DFT as a periodic sequence of impulses and just apply the normal transform. You can also interpret the DFT as the DTFT operating on a finitely supported discrete sequence. The math is the same but you just compute it at a finite grid in frequency space. This is why zero padding increases your frequency resolution or interpolates in the frequency domain.

We just need to show that matrix F is always (for any positive integer N) invertible. That can be proved in a number of ways. E.g. showing that det(F)!=0 or showing linear independence of the columns of F is sufficient.
